title: Bayern Munich 1 PSG 1 (5-6 agg): Can Arsenal stop Kvaratskhelia in final? Why were Bayern denied penalty?
author: Sebastian Stafford-Bloor
content:
How do you follow one of the greatest Champions League games of all time?

Well, an early goal should help.

After last week’s 5-4 thriller in the first leg between Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain, the return leg of the Champions League semi-final began with Ousame Dembele extending the French club’s lead to 6-4 on aggregate.

The rest of the first half was quite open, with PSG winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia again showing why he is so feared. Controversy surrounded two first-half decisions, where Bayern felt they could have had a penalty and PSG could have received a red card, but both appeals were dismissed by the referee.

In the second half, Harry Kane scored a late goal for Bayern but PSG showed that as well as a brilliant attack, they can also defend and shut out an opponent.

And the team who will need to find a way through are Arsenal, who Luis Enrique’s will face in the final on May 30 in Budapest. PSG beat Mikel Arteta’s side in last year’s semi-finals.

Seb Stafford-Bloor, Nick Miller and Anantaajith Raghuraman break down the action.

Ben White isn’t exactly obsessed with football, famously. It’s a job he’s very good at, but it doesn’t consume him like it does some others, so there’s every chance that he wasn’t watching Bayern vs PSG.

Which might be just as well, because he might have lost valuable sleep had he closely studied the man he’ll almost certainly be marking in the final.

Kvicha Kvaratshkelia is a unique talent, a terrifying combination of finesse and power that is incredibly difficult for even the best defences to deal with. He’s the sort of player a manager will create special plans to deal with, so you wonder whether Mikel Arteta might do something rare and tweak his system, perhaps try and bolster his right side somehow to stop the sort of moment that Kvaratskhelia produced to give PSG the lead in the third minute.

Dayot Upemecano paused for a fraction of a fraction of a second, but that was long enough for Kvaratskhelia to spin around him and leave the defender scrambling. The Frenchman being out of position also meant that Konrad Laimer had to move inside to cover the space, which in turn left Dembele relatively free to pick his spot for the finish.

It’s at moments like this that the bandy-legged Georgian can look utterly unstoppable. Good luck, Ben.

Nick Miller

Given the decision to penalise Alphonso Davies for handball in last week’s game (see below) and award PSG a penalty, the failure to punish Joao Neves this evening baffled — and infuriated — Allianz Arena. Neves’ touch was inadvertent and it was from a rushed clearance made by Vitinha, his own teammate, but his arm was extended out from his body.

Waving away the Bayern protests, the referee seemed to indicate that the ball struck Neves high on the arm, near the shoulder, but it was closer to his forearm and seemed a more blatant incident than the one that occurred at Parc des Princes.

But according to the current interpretation of the law, the referee got the decision right, even if the reasons why were not communicated entirely clearly. If a handball occurs after the ball is kicked by one of the culpable player’s team-mates, then there is an exemption.

Seb Stafford-Bloor

The temptation is always to second-guess the losing head coach, but that would hardly be fair on Vincent Kompany. He picked the side everyone else would have selected. His team played with the shape and the same mechanisms they have been using all season, with tremendous success.

Not every defeat needs a post-mortem, especially not when it comes at the hands of such a talented opponent.

The shame of it for Kompany will be in some of the inconvenient detail and the what-might-have-beens.

Serge Gnabry’s injury has been a tough blow to take. Jamal Musiala is still not at his best and has been unable to replace him. Lennart Karl, Bayern’s brilliant teenager, was only just passed fit for this game and was therefore not the match-changer he might have been.

These are fact-of-life issues for any coach but, combined with a magnificent defensive performance from PSG, they were of great significance. It’s rare to say this, but it’s hard to think of anything else Kompany could or should have done.

Seb Stafford-Bloor

Often, the best teams in Europe don’t reach the Champions League final, but this season they probably have.

Arsenal have been the most consistent in the competition, but PSG unquestionably look like the most complete side on the continent, something they displayed emphatically in the second leg against Bayern.

Their defence, marshalled by Marquinhos, is tight, broadly because they tend to defend as a team: it was notable that when Bayern attacked, PSG frequently had nine or 10 players behind the ball. At one point, Bradley Barcola, nominally their central attacker, found himself as a second right-back.

Their midfield is a whirling carousel, moving the ball around at dizzying speeds: Vitinha, Joao Neves and Fabian Ruiz will pass you to death and provide their attack the opportunity to feast on the remains.

Not that the attack necessarily needs it: stop Kvaratshkelia and you’ve got Ousmane Dembele to deal with, keep him out and either Barcola or Desire Doue will get you.

Arguably, their only genuine weakness is in goal, where Matvey Safonov doesn’t inspire confidence. But the ball has to reach him for that to be a problem, and that frequently doesn’t happen.

Nick Miller

The great takeaway from tonight was that PSG have proved they can win in multiple ways.

The defining feature of PSG — as with any Luis Enrique team — is their fluidity with and without the ball. Their front six can pop up all over the pitch, their full-backs often get into goalscoring positions and their centre-backs are not afraid to push further up the pitch.

Simultaneously, PSG can defend with a stout rearguard that leaves no gaps, embrace the dark arts, celebrate tackles and fouls won and beat teams down on the counter-attack, which proved their blueprint in Munich.

How will Arsenal’s back four, plus the work rate of Declan Rice, deal with those rotations? Physicality will be their friend but may not be enough. If PSG limit their progression out of the back with a suffocating and coordinated press, Arsenal could struggle.

Simultaneously, Matvey Safonov often seems flappable in goal and Arsenal’s set pieces could cause issues. Bukayo Saka, if he is back to his best, and Kai Havertz, if he starts, will be vital in the half-spaces.

Storylines aplenty — we are in for a tense, but cracking final.
